title: West End Roof Garden days and the Columbia recording contract
summary: All-night party jobs, rehearsals with Newcomb girls, then Columbia asks for an original number and the band later records 15 sides in Atlanta.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: at this party, was having a Cafe Bulo party, at Tranchinas, which was at, Millenburg, at that, or Spanish Fort. We went out there, and played till about ten o'clock, that next day, it was one of the most rugged nights, we ever had in our lives. But we had some wonderful times, playing on that West End Roof Garden. One of the things, that was so enjoyable about it, we used to go out every afternoon, at two o'clock, and rehearse. A lot of the girls from Newcomb, would come out there, to listen to us rehearse. Being all single boys, and some of them that were, thinking about college, and so forth, half the band would be, rehearsing one, one number, the other half dancing, and then the other half would, rehearse, and the other half would dance. So we really enjoyed our work, I'll tell you that. And I just don't recall, how this recording started, I don't recall, but we were contacted, by the Columbia Recording Company, to make a record. And as I understand it, as I remember it, they wanted an original number. And that's how the Owl's Hoot, came into being, along with Oh Me, Oh My, which was not an original number. And those were the first two, that we recorded. And about, I think it was two years later, we were packed up, and sent to Atlanta, where we made all the rest, of these recordings that we have. I think there's a total, of 15 recordings, all together. But those recordings, were, except for, Eccentric, and West End Romp, were music, that was sent to us, by the, by the Columbia Recording Company, and we were told, that was what we were to play. Frankly, I don't like any of them, except the, Eccentric, and the few that we, we were just ad-libbing, and playing that way. But, we played them, I don't think they ever, any of them ever went over too well, although, there's an awful lot of talk about them, still going on, and occasionally we hear them on the radio, when they talk about old timers. But you know, it's a funny thing, when we started playing, there were very, very few, uh, uh, white bands, in existence. Most all of them, and the good jazz bands, were really colored, colored jazz bands. And, it was a little, it was a peculiar feeling, for us to break into this, uh, jazz field here, uh, under those conditions. Now, you want to rub that out, you can rub,
